placate

/PLAY-kayt/ - the stress falls on PLAY · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Placate means to ease the anger of, soothe.

A tray of free samples at the door did little to placate the neighbors after the bakery's mixers ran all night.

Example

When the venue moved the concert indoors at the last minute, the promoter tried to placate furious ticket holders with front-row upgrades and signed posters—an hour later the line at the refund window had thinned to nothing.

Placate points at a person's anger and works to lower it, usually with a gesture: the upgrade, the discount, the apology. It is more targeted than 'calm'—you calm nerves or a crowd in any mood, but you placate someone who is angry at you.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conciliate: Conciliate aims past the outburst at the relationship itself — a conciliating manager wants the two sides working together again, not merely quiet. Placate has the narrower job of taking the heat out of someone's present anger, usually with a gesture. You placate to end a scene; you conciliate to mend the bond.

mollify: Mollify means to soften someone's anger, often only partly — a small apology mollifies without fully satisfying. Placate is more transactional: a concrete gesture — the free dessert, the comped repair — offered so the anger will stand down. Mollify takes the edge off the mood; placate answers the grievance with amends.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enrage: pushes someone into fury

antagonize: stirs up hostility on purpose

Where it sits · how much you concede to quiet anger — calm → placate → appease

calm vs. placate: Calm is the mildest and most general word here — you can calm a nervous friend who isn't angry at anyone at all, while you placate someone whose anger is aimed squarely at you.

appease vs. placate: Appease goes further than calm or placate—the appeaser pays for quiet, granting the angry side what it demands and hoping the bill stops there.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — plac

Root — plac: to calm, to please (Latin placare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to act

Put it together

Put it together: Plac- (to calm, from Latin placare) + -ate (verb-maker) = to make calm. Placare is the action twin of placere, 'to please'—the root behind placid and complacent in this same unit: placate works to produce the calm that placid names.

Use the root in a new word: placebo

Use the root in a new word: placebo: Regulators required the company to report results from the placebo group alongside everyone else's.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Placate is the everyday verb for taking the heat out of someone's anger with a gesture. Its unit-mates divide the work: assuage eases the feeling itself (you assuage anger, but placate the angry person); appease, in the reference list, is placate with the price paid in concessions; conciliate (a chip above) aims at repairing the whole relationship. If no one is actually angry, you want 'calm,' not placate.
